claim: Respiratory syncytial virus is the leading cause of lower respiratory tract infection among infants.
source: Respiratory syncytial virus is the leading cause of lower respiratory tract infection among infants.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Nair et al., 2010 in the Introduction section.

claim: A 50% reduction in RSV hospitalisations is possible if the maternal vaccine effectiveness can achieve 75 days of additional protection for newborns combined with a 75% coverage of their birth household co-inhabitants (~7.5% population coverage).
source: We find that a 50% reduction in RSV hospitalisations is possible if the maternal vaccine effectiveness can achieve 75 days of additional protection for newborns combined with a 75% coverage of their birth household co-inhabitants (~7.5% population coverage).
evidence: This claim is based on model predictions using inferred parameters from RSV hospitalization data.

claim: A large majority of children contract RSV by the age of two.
source: A large majority of children contract RSV by the age of two (Glezen et al., 1986; Ohuma et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Glezen et al., 1986 and Ohuma et al., 2012.

claim: The chance of developing severe disease from a RSV infection is much greater amongst young infants (6 months) and decreases rapidly with the age of the infected child.
source: but the chance of developing severe disease from a RSV infection is much greater amongst young infants (6 months) (Hall et al., 2009) and decreases rapidly with the age of the infected child.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hall et al., 2009.

claim: There are over 40 RSV vaccines in development as of December 2018.
source: As of December 2018, there are over 40 RSV vaccines in development (PATH, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to PATH, 2018.

claim: Two vaccination approaches have been identified as potentially effective: a single dose vaccine aimed at mothers-to-be leading to antibody transfer across the placenta thereby boosting maternally acquired immunity among newborns, and paediatric vaccination aimed directly at infants.
source: In particular, two vaccination approaches have been identified as potentially effective: a single dose vaccine aimed at mothers-to-be leading to antibody transfer across the placenta thereby boosting maternally acquired immunity among newborns, and paediatric vaccination aimed directly at infants (Modjarrad et al., 2016; World Health Organization, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Modjarrad et al., 2016 and World Health Organization, 2017.

claim: A prophylactic extended half-life monoclonal antibody could act as a vaccine surrogate whilst replicating the desired effect of a maternal vaccine.
source: Moreover, it is possible that a prophylactic extended half-life monoclonal antibody could act as a vaccine surrogate whilst replicating the desired effect of a maternal vaccine (Zhu et al., 2017; Domachowske et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Zhu et al., 2017 and Domachowske et al., 2018.

claim: A serious complication in RSV vaccine development has historically been the risk of causing enhanced disease amongst the immunologically naive.
source: A serious complication in RSV vaccine development has historically been the risk of causing enhanced disease amongst the immunologically naive (Chin et al., 1969)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Chin et al., 1969.

claim: Older individuals (elder siblings, parents) are potential sources of infection for the infant of the household.
source: Epidemiological data suggests older individuals (elder siblings, parents) are potential sources of infection for the infant of the household (Graham, 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Graham, 2014.

claim: The majority of RSV infections among young infants originated from within their household rather than the wider community, with older siblings being the usual household index case.
source: Molecular analysis of nasopharyngeal samples collected from a semi-rural community in Kenya has identified that the majority of RSV infections among young infants originated from within their household rather than the wider community, with older siblings being the usual household index case (Munywoki et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Munywoki et al., 2014.

claim: The young infant was herself the index case on a significant number of occasions.
source: although it should also be noted that the young infant was herself the index case on a significant number of occasions.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the cited study (Munywoki et al., 2014).

claim: There are very high rates of prenatal contact between pregnant women and health professionals in Kenya (97.5% in Kilifi county).
source: In Kenya, there are very high rates of prenatal contact between pregnant women and health professionals (97.5% in Kilifi county; KNBS, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to KNBS, 2015.

claim: The only reported phase III trial on RSV vaccine effectiveness is for the maternally targeted ResVax, which failed to meet its primary objective but nonetheless showed partial effectiveness at reducing hospitalisations due to RSV.
source: At this time, the only reported phase III trial on RSV vaccine effectiveness is for the maternally targeted ResVax, which failed to meet its primary objective but nonetheless showed partial effectiveness at reducing hospitalisations due to RSV (NovaVax, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to NovaVax, 2019.

claim: The model inferred that the mean period of protection against RSV after birth due to transplacental transfer of antibodies from mother to baby is 21.6 days on average.
source: The rapid increase in per-capita infection rate was due to waning of maternally acquired immunity to RSV, which we inferred as lasting on average 21.6 days ([17.2, 26.1] 95% CI; see Table 3 for all inferred parameters).
evidence: This claim is based on parameter inference from hospitalization data.

claim: School age children suffered on average the highest force of infection from outside of the household followed by under 1 year olds.
source: We found that, pre-vaccination, school age children suffered on average the highest force of infection, that is the per-capita rate of infectious contacts, from outside of the household followed by under 1 year olds (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is based on model predictions shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The highest per-capita rates of infection within households were for 7 year olds.
source: The highest per-capita rates of infection within households were for 7 year olds (Figure 3C)
evidence: This claim is based on model predictions shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The total infection rate within households was greatest in size 5 and 6 households.
source: The total infection rate within households was greatest in size 5 and 6 households (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is based on model predictions shown in Figure 3D.

claim: At KCH all RSV hospitalisations occurred in the under five year olds with 84% of hospitalisations occurring in the under 1 year olds.
source: At KCH all RSV hospitalisations occurred in the under five year olds with 84% of hospitalisations occurring in the under 1 year olds (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is based on observed hospitalization data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: A 16% increase in under ones in the population occurred between 2002-2009.
source: A general trend of increasing hospitalisations between 2002–2009 is at least partially explained by a 16% increase in under ones in the population over that period.
evidence: This claim is based on demographic data from the KHDSS.

claim: If the MAB vaccine was unavailable or ineffective (0 days MAB protection), it was still possible to reduce RSV hospitalisations by up to 25% using only the IRP vaccine on the household members of young infants at time of birth.
source: If the MAB vaccine was unavailable or ineffective (0 days MAB protection), we found that it was still possible to reduce RSV hospitalisations by up to 25% using only the IRP vaccine on the household members of young infants at time of birth (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This claim is based on model predictions shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: If 100% maternal vaccination could be achieved then the MAB vaccine was more successful as a sole vaccine option compared to IRP vaccination; 90 days of additional protection from RSV delivered a 45% reduction in hospitalisation even with no IRP vaccine coverage.
source: If 100% maternal vaccination could be achieved then the MAB vaccine was more successful as a sole vaccine option compared to IRP vaccination; in the sense that 90 days of additional protection from RSV delivered a 45% reduction in hospitalisation even with no IRP vaccine coverage.
evidence: This claim is based on model predictions.

claim: A greater than 50% reduction in hospitalisations was achieved with a MAB vaccine that gave 75 additional days of RSV protection and a 75% coverage of the pregnant womens' households.
source: Nonetheless, even with an effective MAB vaccine there was added benefit to also using a IRP vaccine; a greater than 50% reduction in hospitalisations was achieved with a MAB vaccine that gave 75 additional days of RSV protection and a 75% coverage of the pregnant womens' households (Figure 4A; a colorblind-friendly version of this plot can be found as appendix 4 Fig D).
evidence: This claim is based on model predictions shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Improving the effectiveness of the MAB vaccine caused a significant improvement in hospitalisations, but had an almost negligible effect on the total infections in the population.
source: Improving the effectiveness of the MAB vaccine caused a significant improvement in hospitalisations, but had an almost negligible effect on the total infections in the population (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: This claim is based on model predictions shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: For the mixed strategy achieving a 50% reduction in RSV hospitalisations (75 days direct MAB protection at 100% MAB coverage with 75% IRP household coverage), the seasonal dynamics of hospitalisations post-vaccination equilibrated rapidly.
source: For the mixed strategy achieving a 50% reduction in RSV hospitalisations described above (75 days direct MAB protection at 100% MAB coverage with 75% IRP household coverage), the seasonal dynamics of hospitalisations post-vaccination equilibrated rapidly (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is based on model predictions shown in Figure 5A.

claim: There was a reduction in median hospitalisations in every age group, but predominantly in 0–3 month years old (who are nearly all protected by the MAB vaccine) and 3–6 month year olds.
source: There was a reduction in median hospitalisations in every age group, but predominantly in 0–3 month years old (who are nearly all protected by the MAB vaccine) and 3–6 month year olds (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is based on model predictions shown in Figure 5B.

claim: As the duration of protection given by the MAB vaccine increased the efficiency of vaccination also increased; significantly for hospitalisations and marginally for infections.
source: Unsurprisingly, as the duration of protection given by the MAB vaccine increased the efficiency of vaccination also increased; significantly for hospitalisations (Figure 6A) and marginally for infections (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is based on model predictions shown in Figure 6A and 6B.

claim: If there is no MAB vaccine available then the efficiency of using only IRP vaccination doesn't change with coverage.
source: If there is no MAB vaccine available then the efficiency of using only IRP vaccination doesn't change with coverage; that is that when increasing IRP household coverage the improvement per vaccine used stayed static, in line with what one might expect from a homogeneous mixing RSV model (see Box 1).
evidence: This claim is based on model predictions and comparison to a simple model.

claim: When MAB and IRP vaccines were used in conjunction there was an efficiency penalty due to redundancy in the each vaccine's protective effect.
source: However, when MAB and IRP vaccines were used in conjunction there was an efficiency penalty due to redundancy in the each vaccine's protective effect.
evidence: This claim is based on model predictions.

claim: Using two types of vaccine always decreased infections and hospitalisations, but the total reduction was always less than simply adding the reductions of each vaccine in the absence of the other.
source: Using two types of vaccine always decreased infections and hospitalisations (see above), but the total reduction was always less than simply adding the reductions of each vaccine in the absence of the other.
evidence: This claim is based on model predictions.

claim: At maximum effective household coverage for the IRP vaccination only ~10% of the population were vaccinated each year with a modest reduction in the RSV infection rate of ~5%.
source: Even at maximum effective household coverage for the IRP vaccination only ~10% of the population were vaccinated each year with a modest reduction in the RSV infection rate of ~5%.
evidence: This claim is based on model predictions.

claim: At maximum effective household coverage for the IRP vaccination, IRP vaccination alone achieved a 25% reduction in hospitalisations at KCH even without an effective MAB vaccine to provide direct protection to young infants.
source: Nonetheless, at that coverage IRP vaccination alone achieved a 25% reduction in hospitalisations at KCH even without an effective MAB vaccine to provide direct protection to young infants.
evidence: This claim is based on model predictions.

claim: The time between recovery from an RSV episode and reversion back to at least partial susceptibility is estimated to be 6 months.
source: The time between recovery from an episode and reversion back to at least partial susceptibility is estimated to be 6 months (Ohuma et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ohuma et al., 2012.

claim: There are sharp annual peaks of RSV hospitalisation at each seasonal RSV epidemic in Kilifi county.
source: In Kilifi county, there are sharp annual peaks of RSV hospitalisation at each seasonal RSV epidemic
evidence: This claim is based on observed hospitalization data.

claim: The seasonality of RSV hospitalisations at KCH has historically been erratic with peak months for RSV hospitalisation varying as widely as November to April.
source: The seasonality of RSV hospitalisations at KCH has historically been erratic with peak months for RSV hospitalisation varying as widely as November to April (appendix 1).
evidence: This claim is based on observed hospitalization data.

claim: Over the 15-year period studied, there was demographic change in the underlying population both in age profile and household size distribution.
source: Moreover, over the 15-year period we are studying in this paper, there was demographic change in the underlying population both in age profile and household size distribution.
evidence: This claim is based on demographic data from the KHDSS.

claim: The model was able to broadly capture the year-to-year variation in hospitalisation, and age profile of the hospitalised, with only six free parameters.
source: We were able to broadly capture the year-to-year variation in hospitalisation, and age profile of the hospitalised, with only six free parameters (Figure 2, Materials and methods, and appendix 1).
evidence: This claim is based on model fitting to hospitalization data.

claim: The 2005/2006 RSV year was anomalous in that there were three peaks in RSV hospitalisation separated by at least a month.
source: The 2005/2006 RSV year (see appendix 1 for RSV year definition) was anomalous in that there were three peaks in RSV hospitalisation separated by at least a month: two smaller peaks on 11th Dec 2005 and 24th Mar 2006 around a larger peak on 24th Feb 2006.
evidence: This claim is based on observed hospitalization data.

claim: Outside of the 2005/2006 RSV year there were 2174 hospitalisations during the period of study compared to a model prediction of 2147 hospitalisations ([2057, 2238] 95% prediction interval).
source: Outside of the 2005/2006 RSV year there were 2174 hospitalisations during the period of study compared to a model prediction of 2147 hospitalisations ([2057, 2238] 95% prediction interval ).
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of observed data to model predictions.

claim: The model assumes that all U1 individuals susceptible to RSV were at risk of their first RSV episode and that all O1 individuals had already been infected at least once.
source: In the model used in this paper, we assumed that all U1 individuals susceptible to RSV were at risk of their first RSV episode and that all O1 individuals had already been infected at least once, since re-infection within the same yearly epidemic is unlikely but nearly everyone has caught RSV by the age of two years old (Glezen et al., 1986).
evidence: This is a model assumption supported by citation to Glezen et al., 1986.

claim: The model assumes that individuals were born with a temporary immunity to RSV which faded over time.
source: The main modifications were consistent with previous RSV transmission models; we assumed that: (i) individuals were born with a temporary immunity to RSV which faded over time
evidence: This is a model assumption consistent with previous RSV models.

claim: The model assumes that RSV infection episodes provide individuals with only temporary protection from re-infection (mean 6 months).
source: and (ii) RSV infection episodes provide individuals with only temporary protection from re-infection (mean 6 months Scott et al., 2006; White et al., 2007; Moore et al., 2014; Pitzer et al., 2015; Kinyanjui et al., 2015; Yamin et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a model assumption supported by multiple citations.

claim: After an initial RSV infection there is evidence that individuals retain reduced susceptibility to subsequent RSV infection.
source: After an initial RSV infection there is evidence that individuals retain reduced susceptibility to subsequent RSV infection (Henderson et al., 1979; Hall et al., 1991)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Henderson et al., 1979 and Hall et al., 1991.

claim: Individuals will potentially have less infectious asymptomatic episodes if infected after an initial RSV infection.
source: and will potentially have less infectious asymptomatic episodes if infected (Hall et al., 2001; Yamin et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hall et al., 2001 and Yamin et al., 2016.

claim: The model assumes that the elicited period of immunity to RSV from receiving the IRP vaccine would be similar to that of a natural infection.
source: We follow (Yamin et al., 2016) in assuming that the elicited period of immunity to RSV from receiving the IRP vaccine would be similar to that of a natural infection.
evidence: This is a model assumption following Yamin et al., 2016.

claim: The model assumes that the maximum coverage of the vaccine would be reached within a year.
source: We assumed that the maximum coverage of the vaccine would be reached within a year, and considered 10 years of RSV transmission after this implementation.
evidence: This is a model assumption.

claim: The model assumes that the total birth rate was constant (8601 per year) for the 10-year forecasting period.
source: However, for the 10-year forecasting in this paper, we assumed that the total birth rate was constant (8601 per year), and that the population age and household occupancy distributions remained static.
evidence: This is a model assumption for forecasting.

claim: The model assumes that if the pregnant mother's household cohabitants agreed to receive an immune response provoking vaccine then all were vaccinated at the birth of the newborn to maximise the overlap between the protection period of the cohabitants and the first months of life of the newborn.
source: We assumed that if the pregnant mother's household cohabitants agreed to receive an immune response provoking vaccine then all were vaccinated at the birth of the newborn to maximise the overlap between the protection period of the cohabitants and the first months of life of the newborn.
evidence: This is a model assumption.

claim: KCH serves as the primary care facility for the KHDSS population.
source: KCH serves as the primary care facility for the KHDSS population, and we assumed that all KHDSS members who accessed urgent hospital treatment due to RSV disease accessed their treatment at KCH.
evidence: This is a model assumption based on knowledge of the healthcare system.

claim: The model assumes that all KHDSS members who accessed urgent hospital treatment due to RSV disease accessed their treatment at KCH.
source: KCH serves as the primary care facility for the KHDSS population, and we assumed that all KHDSS members who accessed urgent hospital treatment due to RSV disease accessed their treatment at KCH.
evidence: This is a model assumption.

claim: The model assumes that the maternal vaccine was delivered as one injection to the pregnant women in her third trimester.
source: We assumed that the maternal vaccine was delivered as one injection to the pregnant women in her third trimester.
evidence: This is a model assumption.

claim: 100% effective coverage of the households where births occurred corresponded to ~10% effective coverage of the total population by 2016.
source: It should be noted that by 2016 the KHDSS population was around 240,000 people, hence 100% effective coverage of the households where births occurred corresponded to ~10% effective coverage of the total population.
evidence: This claim is based on demographic data and calculation.

claim: Over 10 years of forecasted RSV epidemics if a MAB vaccine was available, and given to every pregnant mother, 8601 MAB vaccines were deployed each year.
source: Over 10 years of forecasted RSV epidemics if a MAB vaccine was available, and given to every pregnant mother, 8601 MAB vaccines were deployed each year.
evidence: This claim is based on model assumptions and demographic data.

claim: 0–24,095 IRP vaccines were deployed each year depending on household coverage.
source: 0–24,095 IRP vaccines were deployed each year depending on household coverage.
evidence: This claim is based on model assumptions and demographic data.

claim: The model inference stage included inferring the statistics of yearly variation in RSV seasonality.
source: The model inference stage included inferring the statistics of yearly variation in RSV seasonality.
evidence: This describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: The decrease in rates of RSV hospitalisation and infection due to vaccination over ten years presented are median improvements over 500 independent realisations of random future seasonal patterns compared to a baseline of no intervention.
source: The decrease in rates of RSV hospitalisation and infection due to vaccination over ten years presented are median improvements over 500 independent realisations of random future seasonal patterns compared to a baseline of no intervention.
evidence: This describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: The model was unable to explain the unusual 2005/2006 RSV year with three peaks.
source: The model was unable to explain this unusual year, other years having solitary peaks.
evidence: This is a limitation of the model fit to data.

claim: Targeting pregnant women and their cohabitants did not prevent sufficient RSV infections as to significantly disrupt RSV transmission within the population at large.
source: However, targeting pregnant women and their cohabitants did not prevent sufficient RSV infections as to significantly disrupt RSV transmission within the population at large, which may explain the rapid approach to new RSV hospitalisation dynamics.
evidence: This claim is based on model predictions.

claim: Those who were protected were overwhelmingly among those at most risk of disease if they had caught RSV.
source: Nonetheless, those who were protected were overwhelmingly among those at most risk of disease if they had caught RSV.
evidence: This claim is based on model predictions.

claim: The combined vaccination strategy was efficient at targeting effort towards directly protecting young infants most at risk of developing RSV disease with boosted antibodies, and filling in any gap in protection with indirect cocoon protection within the household using a vaccine aimed at older cohabitants.
source: We found that the combined vaccination strategy was efficient at targeting effort towards directly protecting young infants most at risk of developing RSV disease with boosted antibodies, and filling in any gap in protection with indirect cocoon protection within the household using a vaccine aimed at older cohabitants.
evidence: This claim is based on model predictions and analysis.

claim: Although vaccinating at a low rate compared to population size, with only a modest reduction in infection rate, those people vaccinated were efficient at cocooning young infants from transmission and therefore risk of severe disease.
source: This demonstrated that although we were vaccinating at a low rate compared to population size, with only a modest reduction in infection rate, those people we did vaccinate were efficient at cocooning young infants from transmission and therefore risk of severe disease.
evidence: This claim is based on model predictions and analysis.

claim: If an effective MAB vaccine was also available the reduction in hospitalisations was greater, although the additional protection due to cocooning was relatively less since young infants were also protected from contracting RSV at the age when they were at most risk of severe disease.
source: If an effective MAB vaccine was also available the reduction in hospitalisations was greater, although the additional protection due to cocooning was relatively less since young infants were also protected from contracting RSV at the age when they were at most risk of severe disease.
evidence: This claim is based on model predictions and analysis.

claim: A cocooning protective effect of households could explain the big discrepancy between the estimate of the mean period of protection against RSV after birth in this study (21.6 days) compared to a RSV transmission modelling study by Kinyanjui et al on the same population using an age-structured model (2.3 months or 4 months depending on contact pattern assumptions).
source: A cocooning protective effect of households could explain the big discrepancy between our estimate of the mean period of protection against RSV after birth due to transplacental transfer of antibodies from mother to baby in the the womb (21.6 days of natural protection on average) compared to a RSV transmission modelling study by Kinyanjui et al on the same population using an age-structured model (Kinyanjui et al., 2015) (2.3 months of natural protection if the age mixing was based on diary estimates of contacts (Kiti et al., 2014) or 4 months of natural protection if the age mixing was based on household co-occupancy and schooling ages).
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of model results to previous studies and inference about model structure effects.

claim: The age-structured model used in the Kinyanjui et al study reported high or very high reproductive ratios: 7.08 for the diary based contact patterns, and 25.60 for the household co-occupancy and schooling age based contact pattern.
source: The age-structured model used in the Kinyanjui et al study reported high or very high reproductive ratios: 7.08 for the diary based contact patterns, and 25.60 for the household co-occupancy and schooling age based contact pattern.
evidence: This claim is based on citation to Kinyanjui et al., 2015.

claim: The fundamental theory of age-structured transmission models for endemic diseases was developed mainly with reference to diseases that induce very long term or lifelong immunity.
source: However, the fundamental theory of age-structured transmission models for endemic diseases was developed mainly with reference to diseases that induce very long term or lifelong immunity (Anderson and May, 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Anderson and May, 1991.

claim: For diseases provoking long-lasting immunity, one would expect most older household members to be immune and therefore household structure to be a relatively less important factor in predicting risk of transmission compared to the age-structured transmission outside of the household.
source: For diseases provoking long-lasting immunity, one would expect most older household members to be immune and therefore household structure to be a relatively less important factor in predicting risk of transmission compared to the age-structured transmission outside of the household.
evidence: This claim is based on theoretical reasoning about disease transmission.

claim: Simulation study of a generic strongly immunizing infection with realistic demography found limited difference in predicted incidence rate by age for people at schooling age or older between models with household structure and age structure compared to models with only age structure.
source: Indeed, simulation study of a generic strongly immunizing infection with realistic demography found limited difference in predicted incidence rate by age for people at schooling age or older between models with household structure and age structure compared to models with only age structure (Geard et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Geard et al., 2015.

claim: The simulation study cited (Geard et al., 2015) predicted that incidence was lower for 0–5 year olds, especially so for under 1 year olds, once household structure was taken into account.
source: However, it is not clear that neglecting household structure is a good approximation for modelling seasonal RSV transmission for two reasons: first, previously infected people lose effective immunological protection to RSV rapidly enough that each season could be closer to an 'epidemic' scenario rather than an 'endemic' scenario. Second, every hospital admission at KCH confirmed as due to RSV was a pre-school aged child; in contrast to predicted incidence rates for school age and older individual, the simulation study cited above (Geard et al., 2015) predicted that incidence was lower for 0–5 year olds, especially so for under 1 year olds, once household structure was taken into account.
evidence: This claim is based on citation to Geard et al., 2015.

claim: The percentage of pregnant women who have at least one prenatal contact in Kilifi county is high (97.5%).
source: The percentage of pregnant women for have at least one prenatal contact in Kilifi county is high (97.5%; KNBS, 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to KNBS, 2015.

claim: It is not clear that prenatal contact always occurs in the mother-to-be's third trimester.
source: however it is not clear that prenatal contact always occurs in the mother-to-be's third trimester.
evidence: This is a statement of uncertainty about the data.

claim: Both the MAB and IRP vaccines are likely to be best deployed late in the pregnancy, in order to maximise direct protection from the MAB vaccine and the duration of indirect protection from the IRP vaccine for the newborn.
source: Both the MAB and IRP vaccines are likely to be best deployed late in the pregnancy, in order to maximise direct protection from the MAB vaccine and the duration of indirect protection from the IRP vaccine for the newborn.
evidence: This claim is based on reasoning about vaccine effectiveness.

claim: RSV hospitalisations have been identified as a crude proxy for the true disease burden.
source: RSV hospitalisations have been identified as a crude proxy for the true disease burden; the passive reporting of RSV hospitalisation can vary for reasons completely independent of RSV epidemiology (Modjarrad et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Modjarrad et al., 2016.

claim: The crude birth rate in Kilifi has followed a declining trend in line with the rest of Kenya.
source: The demography in Kilifi will continue to change in the future, the crude birth rate in Kilifi has followed a declining trend in line with the rest of Kenya.
evidence: This claim is based on demographic data.

claim: The declining crude birth rate leads to a total birth rate which is much closer to static (~8500 births per year).
source: However, this leads to a total birth rate which is much closer to static (~8500 births per year), and therefore the number of at-risk under-ones has been approximately static since 2009.
evidence: This claim is based on demographic data and calculation.

claim: The number of at-risk under-ones has been approximately static since 2009.
source: However, this leads to a total birth rate which is much closer to static (~8500 births per year), and therefore the number of at-risk under-ones has been approximately static since 2009.
evidence: This claim is based on demographic data and calculation.

claim: Combining partially effective vaccines can be complementary in a household-structured setting.
source: We have demonstrated that, all other things be equal, combining partially effective vaccines can be complementary in a household-structured setting.
evidence: This claim is based on model predictions and analysis.

claim: The duration of natural protection to RSV that newborns inherit from their mother was likely to be much shorter than previously estimated.
source: Two central insights from our study were that the duration of natural protection to RSV that newborns inherit from their mother was likely to be much shorter than previously estimated
evidence: This claim is based on model inference from data.

claim: RSV attack rates within the household were significant in maintaining RSV transmission.
source: and that RSV attack rates within the household were significant in maintaining RSV transmission.
evidence: This claim is based on model predictions.

claim: Targeting pregnant women and their households for RSV vaccination is likely to be an effective and efficient strategy under a wide range of different scenarios.
source: Therefore, targeting pregnant women and their households for RSV vaccination is likely to be an effective and efficient strategy under a wide range of different scenarios.
evidence: This claim is based on model predictions across multiple scenarios.

claim: The model used in this paper simulated infection and transmission of RSV among a population described by the Kilifi Demographic and Health surveillance system (KHDSS) between September 2001 and September 2016.
source: The dynamical RSV model used in this paper simulated infection and transmission of RSV among a population described by the Kilifi Demographic and Health surveillance system (KHDSS Scott et al., 2012) between September 2001 and September 2016.
evidence: This describes the model and data used in the study.

claim: The population was assumed to mix and transmit RSV at two social levels: within their household and outside their household among the wider community.
source: The population was assumed to mix and transmit RSV at two social levels: within their household and outside their household among the wider community.
evidence: This is a model assumption.

claim: There were 1926 possible household configurations in the RSV transmission model.
source: There were 1926 possible household configurations in the RSV transmission model.
evidence: This describes the model structure.

claim: The model included only households of total size ten or less with two or fewer under ones.
source: In order to limit the number of possible household states, we included only households of total size ten or less with two or fewer under ones.
evidence: This is a model design choice.

claim: The household size limits were chosen based on capturing ≈99% of the U1s in the population.
source: We chose these limits on the household size based on capturing ≈99% of the U1s in the population, and therefore the pathway to them catching RSV (appendix 2).
evidence: This is a model design choice based on data.

claim: The data for parameter inference was RSV-confirmed, age-specific weekly admissions to Kilifi county hospital (KCH) hospitalisation data from September 2001 until September 2016.
source: The data for parameter inference was RSV-confirmed, age-specific weekly admissions to Kilifi county hospital (KCH) hospitalisation data from September 2001 until September 2016 (see Nokes et al., 2009 for study details).
evidence: This describes the data used for model inference.

claim: A significant number of admissions were from people not within the KHDSS survey leading to data re-scaling.
source: However, a significant number of admissions were from people not within the KHDSS survey leading to data re-scaling (see appendix 3).
evidence: This describes a data processing step.

claim: The log-likelihood for a particular simulation corresponded to Poisson errors.
source: The log-likelihood for a particular simulation corresponded to Poisson errors
evidence: This describes the statistical model used for inference.

claim: The Expectation-maximisation (EM) algorithm was used to converge onto maximum likelihood estimates for the four free parameters, and the two hyperparameters of the log-seasonality model.
source: Therefore, we treated the yearly variation in seasonality as missing data and used the Expectation-maximisation (EM) algorithm (Dempster et al., 1977) to converge onto maximum likelihood estimates for the four free parameters, and the two hyperparameters of the log-seasonality model
evidence: This describes the inference methodology.

claim: 95% confidence intervals were constructed using the likelihood profile technique.
source: 95% confidence intervals were constructed using the likelihood profile technique (e.g. King et al., 2008 and appendix 3).

claim: The model was initialized by starting with a completely susceptible population with the population demography set to mimic that of the KHDSS on 1st Jan 2000.
